items.title: A poet on the assembly line
items.dek: Xiao Hai left Henan for Shenzhen's factories at fifteen and spent his youth on production lines. His memoir, Adrift in the South, now in English, is less a catalogue of suffering than a record of how a migrant worker held on to beauty, and a test of how Western readers choose to read Chinese labour.
paragraphs: Every smartphone and sweatshirt carries an invisible biography, and only rarely does the person who made it get to write that biography down. Xiao Hai, born in 1987 in Shangqiu in Henan province, is one of those who did. At fifteen, according to his publisher, his family paid a vocational-school teacher 1,200 yuan to place him in a factory in Shenzhen, and he went on to spend the better part of his youth moving between garment mills and electronics plants in China's booming south. His memoir of those years, Adrift in the South, was published in June 2026 by Granta Magazine Editions in a translation by Tony Hao.

The book has an unusual genealogy. Its first chapter began life as an essay Xiao Hai wrote in 2019 and posted online in Chinese; Hao translated it for Granta's 2024 issue on contemporary Chinese writing, and the full memoir was commissioned on the strength of it. The English edition, in other words, arrives before the Chinese one, which Public Books reports is due to appear in China this year. That sequence is a small parable in itself about who gets to circulate a migrant worker's story, and in which markets it first finds a price.

What the book records is the familiar architecture of China's internal migration: crowded dormitories, long shifts, abusive bosses and venal officials, and wages of roughly 2,000 yuan a month. The review in Public Books singles out one detail that does the work of an entire treatise on value. A Nike sweatshirt of the kind Xiao Hai once sewed sold in Beijing for around 700 yuan, close to two weeks of his pay. Yet the reviewer's central claim is that the memoir is not principally a chronicle of injury. Its real subject is the stubborn pursuit of poetry, landscape and beauty by a young man whose time had been sold, hour by hour, to a machine.

That pursuit is well documented. Xiao Hai started studying poetry at seventeen and, by his account, turned to contemporary free verse in his mid-twenties; the Leeds Centre for New Chinese Writing credits him with more than 500 poems written during his factory years, and his collections include Factory Howl, from 2016, and Sisyphus on the Wenyu River. He is now associated with the Picun literature group, a circle of migrant-worker writers on the outskirts of Beijing, and runs a poetry-themed second-hand clothing shop there, a job that leaves him time to write. In the memoir, his poems serve as epigraphs to the chapters, so that the lyric voice frames the prose rather than being smuggled into it.

The most pointed part of the review concerns reception. The reviewer cautions against the temptation, strong in Anglophone media, to read a book like this purely as an indictment of the Chinese state, noting that the Wall Street Journal ran an excerpt in April. The products Xiao Hai assembled were destined largely for Western shelves, and the review argues that his book belongs to a history of global capitalism and the international movement of goods and power, not to a story about one authoritarian government alone. It places him beside Joseph Ponthus, whose On the Line chronicled French factory shifts, and Matthew Rice, whose collection plastic appeared this year, and asks whether something in industrial labour itself drives workers towards verse.

That question deserves to be taken seriously, and here interpretation must take over from reporting. One plausible answer is that the poem is the form most compatible with stolen time: it can be composed in fragments, held in memory on the line and finished at night. Another is political. To insist on beauty while doing work designed to be anonymous is to refuse the idea that a worker is merely a cost of production. Read this way, Adrift in the South is not an exotic dispatch from somewhere else but a document of the supply chains that pass through every reader's wardrobe, and its author is less a victim to be pitied than a writer to be read on his own terms.

items.grammar: Note the cleft-like frame 'It is not X but Y' and its variants ('is not principally a chronicle of injury. Its real subject is…'; 'is not an exotic dispatch… but a document of…'). Analytical prose uses this contrast to correct a likely misreading before stating the writer's thesis.
questions: Why does the essay call the English edition appearing before the Chinese one 'a small parable'?
What two explanations does the final paragraph offer for why factory workers turn to poetry?
Why does the review resist reading the memoir only as a critique of the Chinese state? Do you find that argument convincing?

items.title: Lesetipps für heute
items.dek: Von der Altersarmut der ersten Gastarbeiter über Sri Lankas Tropenmoderne bis zu Amy Winehouse – sechs Texte zu Migration, Architektur, Film, Musik, Kunst und Gesellschaft.

picks.title: Altersarmut betrifft viele türkische Gastarbeiter
picks.en: Part of a series marking 65 years of the German–Turkish recruitment agreement: a fact-based look at why so many of the first 'guest workers' now face poverty in old age. A sober counterpoint to the usual integration debate.
picks.zh: 德土招工协定65周年：许多第一代土耳其“客籍工人”晚年陷入贫困。

picks.title: Er spannte das Dach einfach zwischen die Felsen
picks.author: Rahel Bueb
picks.en: A portrait of Geoffrey Bawa, the Sri Lankan architect whose buildings grow out of landscape and climate rather than fighting them. A good way into 'tropical modernism' and architecture beyond the Western canon.
picks.zh: 斯里兰卡建筑师杰弗里·巴瓦：让建筑顺应山石与气候。

picks.title: „Kapital und Technik werfen uns unter die Räder“
picks.author: Patrick Heidmann
picks.en: The South Korean director Lee Chang-dong ('Burning', 'Poetry') talks about his new work and about how capital and technology grind people down. Worth it for one of cinema's most thoughtful voices on class.
picks.zh: 韩国导演李沧东访谈：资本与技术如何碾压普通人。

picks.title: Es gibt noch was zu holen im Bienenkorb
picks.author: Nina Apin
picks.en: Twenty years after Amy Winehouse's 'Back to Black', a re-listening that asks what is still to be discovered in the album beyond the myth and the beehive hairdo.
picks.zh: 《Back to Black》二十周年：重听艾米·怀恩豪斯。

picks.title: Der lange Schatten über dem größten Museum der Schweiz
picks.author: Jeni Fulton
picks.en: Why the Bührle collection – built partly on Nazi-era loot and arms-trade money – still unsettles the Kunsthaus Zürich, and why its future funding is now in doubt. A sharp case study in museums and historical responsibility.
picks.zh: 布尔勒收藏与纳粹掠夺艺术：苏黎世美术馆的长久阴影。

picks.title: Warum brannte Paris? Wer das verstehen will, muss eine Vorschule in Pantin besuchen
picks.author: Romy Straßenburg
picks.en: Behind France's recent riots and curfews lies the anger of young people in neglected suburbs; this reportage goes to a preschool in Pantin to trace where it starts. Inequality and public neglect seen from the ground up.
picks.zh: 巴黎为何燃烧？从潘坦一所幼儿园看被忽视郊区的青年怒火。

items.title: Today's reading list
items.dek: Detained abuse survivors, John Berger's way of looking, a housing-crisis film, spirit art against patriarchy, an Abenaki bassist and the rivers we dammed.

picks.title: These Women Were Trying to Escape Domestic Abuse. ICE Detained Them Instead.
picks.author: Melissa Sanchez, Anna Clark
picks.en: Immigrant women who called the police on abusive partners ended up arrested and handed to ICE, some never charged. A long, careful investigation into how weakened victim protections now keep survivors from seeking help.
picks.zh: 报警求助的移民家暴受害女性反被移民局拘押。

picks.outlet: The New York Times Magazine (via Longreads)
picks.title: The Man Who Taught Us How to Pay Attention
picks.author: A.O. Scott
picks.en: Longreads' pick: A.O. Scott on the critic John Berger, whose ways of seeing it presents as an antidote to an age of endless scrolling. A fine essay on attention, images and art.
picks.zh: A.O.斯科特谈约翰·伯格：在无尽刷屏时代学会凝视。

picks.title: I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning: the British housing crisis is ever present in Clio Barnard's touching story of a Birmingham friendship group
picks.author: B. Ruby Rich
picks.en: B. Ruby Rich on Clio Barnard's new film about a working-class circle of friends in Birmingham, where the loss of affordable homes and shared life hangs over every scene. Film criticism that is also social criticism.
picks.zh: 克里奥·巴纳德新片影评：伯明翰工人阶级友谊与住房危机。

picks.title: Spirits Against the Patriarchy
picks.author: Eliza Swann
picks.en: A review of a New York show of seventeen women artists who made work through contact with spirits – and how the Surrealists borrowed their 'automatic' methods while stripping out the spiritual and feminist edge.
picks.zh: 十七位以“通灵”创作的女性艺术家，与反父权的艺术史。

picks.title: Bassist and Composer Mali Obomsawin Builds a Bridge Across Time
picks.en: A feature on the Abenaki bassist and composer Mali Obomsawin and her new album 'Automatic', music that connects Indigenous history with free jazz. Read it with the record playing.
picks.zh: 阿布纳基族贝斯手马莉·奥博姆萨温与新专辑《Automatic》。

picks.title: Death by a Thousand Dams
picks.author: Ben Goldfarb
picks.en: Longreads' pick: Ben Goldfarb on the tens of thousands of small dams in the northeastern US that block migrating fish from recovering. Nature writing about what we never noticed we built.
picks.zh: 美国东北部数以万计的小水坝阻断鱼类洄游。

items.title: Ein Dorf und seine Lücken
items.dek: Shida Bazyar hat mit „Die Lücken“ den Deutschen Buchpreis 2026 gewonnen – einen Roman über Schweigen, Täter und Geflüchtete in einem Hunsrück-Dorf. Die Kritik streitet, ob die Jury eher die Botschaft als die Form ausgezeichnet hat.
paragraphs: Am Abend des 5. Oktober, am Vorabend der Frankfurter Buchmesse, wurde im Kaisersaal des Frankfurter Römers der Deutsche Buchpreis 2026 vergeben. Er ging an Shida Bazyar für ihren Roman „Die Lücken“, erschienen Anfang September bei Kiepenheuer & Witsch. Die Auszeichnung ist mit 25.000 Euro dotiert; die fünf übrigen Autorinnen und Autoren der Shortlist erhalten je 2.500 Euro. Die siebenköpfige Jury hatte zuvor 205 Titel gesichtet.

Schauplatz des knapp 500 Seiten starken Buches ist Heimesbach, ein erfundenes Dorf im Hunsrück, das an Bazyars Geburtsort Hermeskeil angelehnt ist. Erzählt wird von einer Ich-Erzählerin, die bei einem Verkehrsunfall gestorben ist. Nach ihrem Tod kehrt sie an den Ort zurück, an den sie als Zehnjährige mit Eltern und älterer Schwester als Geflüchtete gekommen war – und weiß nun, was das Dorf über seine NS-Vergangenheit verschweigt.

Der Roman umspannt fast ein Jahrhundert. Jüdische Familien, die aus dem Dorf verschwinden, Profiteure des NS-Regimes und kurdische und iranische Menschen, die in Deutschland Schutz suchen, begegnen sich darin über die Zeiten hinweg. Die Jury hob die kaleidoskopartige Bauweise hervor, die zwischen den Epochen springt und reale mit erfundenen Figuren mischt, und nannte das Buch einen Roman gegen Gleichgültigkeit.

Bazyar, 1988 in Rheinland-Pfalz geboren und Tochter iranischer Eltern, debütierte 2016 mit „Nachts ist es leise in Teheran“; ihr zweiter Roman „Drei Kameradinnen“ stand 2021 auf der Longlist desselben Preises. Bei der Verleihung sprach sie laut Börsenblatt von einem merkwürdigen Gefühl, für ein Buch über Verfolgte und Ermordete geehrt zu werden. Zugleich warnte sie vor rassistischen Straftaten: Derzeit habe keine Minderheit in Deutschland keinen Grund zur Sorge.

Nicht alle Kritiker sind restlos überzeugt. Björn Hayer nennt den Roman im Freitag politisch wichtig, findet die Sprache aber zu konventionell und das Thema nicht neu; andere Autorinnen hätten ähnliches Terrain mit größerer künstlerischer Wucht erkundet. Seine Vermutung: Die Jury habe die Botschaft höher gewichtet als die Form – in einer Buchbranche, die zunehmend unter Druck von rechts steht.

Man kann diese Debatte auch anders lesen. Dass ein Roman, der die Geschichte der Täter im eigenen Dorf mit der Ankunft Geflüchteter verknüpft, ausgerechnet jetzt den wichtigsten deutschsprachigen Romanpreis erhält, ist selbst ein Kommentar zur Gegenwart. Ob „Die Lücken“ auch literarisch Bestand hat, werden die Leserinnen und Leser entscheiden – die Frage, die das Buch stellt, nämlich wer im Dorf hinsieht und wer wegschaut, bleibt in jedem Fall offen.
paragraphs_en: On the evening of 5 October, the eve of the Frankfurt Book Fair, the German Book Prize 2026 was awarded in the Kaisersaal of Frankfurt's Römer. It went to Shida Bazyar for her novel "Die Lücken" (The Gaps), published in early September by Kiepenheuer & Witsch. The prize is worth 25,000 euros; the five other shortlisted authors receive 2,500 euros each. The seven-member jury had previously reviewed 205 titles.

The setting of the nearly 500-page book is Heimesbach, a fictional village in the Hunsrück modelled on Bazyar's birthplace, Hermeskeil. The story is told by a first-person narrator who has died in a road accident. After her death she returns to the place where she arrived as a ten-year-old refugee with her parents and older sister – and now knows what the village keeps silent about its Nazi past.

The novel spans almost a century. Jewish families who disappear from the village, profiteers of the Nazi regime, and Kurdish and Iranian people seeking protection in Germany meet in it across the eras. The jury highlighted the kaleidoscopic structure, which jumps between periods and mixes real and invented characters, and called the book a novel against indifference.

Bazyar, born in 1988 in Rhineland-Palatinate to Iranian parents, made her debut in 2016 with "Nachts ist es leise in Teheran" (The Nights Are Quiet in Tehran); her second novel, "Drei Kameradinnen" (Three Comrades), was on the longlist for the same prize in 2021. At the ceremony, according to Börsenblatt, she spoke of the strange feeling of being honoured for a book about people who were persecuted and murdered. At the same time she warned about racist crimes: at present, she said, there is no minority in Germany that has no reason to worry.

Not all critics are fully convinced. Writing in Freitag, Björn Hayer calls the novel politically important but finds its language too conventional and its subject not new; other women writers, he argues, have explored similar ground with greater artistic force. His suspicion: the jury weighted the message more heavily than the form – in a book industry increasingly under pressure from the right.

One can also read this debate differently. That a novel linking the history of the perpetrators in one's own village with the arrival of refugees should win the most important German-language novel prize precisely now is itself a comment on the present. Whether "Die Lücken" lasts as literature is for readers to decide – but the question the book asks, namely who in the village looks and who looks away, remains open either way.

to weight, to give priority to

items.grammar: Reported speech with Konjunktiv I: "Derzeit habe keine Minderheit … keinen Grund zur Sorge" and "Die Jury habe die Botschaft höher gewichtet" use habe instead of hat to signal that the writer is reporting someone else's claim, not asserting it. 【间接引语用第一虚拟式，表示转述他人观点】
questions: Warum wählt Bazyar wohl eine tote Erzählerin, die mehr weiß als die Lebenden?
Sollte ein Literaturpreis eher die Form oder eher die Botschaft eines Romans auszeichnen? Begründen Sie Ihre Meinung.
Was verbindet im Roman die NS-Vergangenheit des Dorfes mit der Ankunft Geflüchteter in den 1990er-Jahren?

items.title: Helgoland gegen Sansibar? Ein Tausch, den es nie gab
items.dek: Bis heute heißt es oft, Deutschland habe 1890 Sansibar gegen Helgoland eingetauscht. Das stimmt so nicht – und die Legende hat einen politischen Ursprung.
paragraphs: Die Nordseeinsel Helgoland war im 19. Jahrhundert britisch – nach Angaben von Planet Wissen seit 1807. Erst am 1. Juli 1890 kam sie durch einen Vertrag zwischen dem Deutschen Reich und Großbritannien zu Deutschland. Im Volksmund heißt dieses Abkommen „Helgoland-Sansibar-Vertrag“, offiziell aber „Vertrag über Kolonien und Helgoland“.

Der Name führt in die Irre: Sansibar war ein unabhängiges Sultanat und nie eine deutsche Kolonie, konnte also gar nicht getauscht werden. Deutschland erkannte im Vertrag nur an, dass Großbritannien die Insel unter seinen Schutz stellen wollte. Außerdem gab das Reich die Kolonie Witu im heutigen Kenia und Ansprüche in Uganda ab. Dafür erhielt es neben Helgoland den sogenannten Caprivizipfel, einen Landstreifen, der Deutsch-Südwestafrika mit dem Fluss Sambesi verband.

Die Legende vom schlechten Tausch stammt von Otto von Bismarck. Wenige Tage nach der Unterzeichnung kritisierte der gerade entlassene Kanzler den Vertrag öffentlich, um seinem Nachfolger Leo von Caprivi zu schaden. Lange erzählte man sich danach, Deutschland habe einen neuen Anzug gegen einen alten Knopf hergegeben. Was dabei meist fehlt: Über die Grenzen in Afrika entschieden zwei europäische Mächte – die Menschen, die dort lebten, wurden nicht gefragt.
paragraphs_en: In the 19th century the North Sea island of Heligoland was British – since 1807, according to Planet Wissen. Only on 1 July 1890 did it pass to Germany through a treaty between the German Empire and Great Britain. Colloquially the agreement is called the "Heligoland–Zanzibar Treaty", but its official name is the "Treaty on Colonies and Heligoland".

The name is misleading: Zanzibar was an independent sultanate and never a German colony, so it could not be swapped at all. In the treaty Germany merely acknowledged that Britain intended to place the island under its protection. The Reich also gave up the colony of Witu in present-day Kenya and claims in Uganda. In return it received, besides Heligoland, the so-called Caprivi Strip, a strip of land that connected German South West Africa with the Zambezi river.

The legend of the bad swap comes from Otto von Bismarck. A few days after the signing, the recently dismissed chancellor publicly criticised the treaty in order to damage his successor, Leo von Caprivi. For a long time afterwards people said Germany had given away a new suit for an old button. What is usually missing: the borders in Africa were decided by two European powers – the people who lived there were not asked.
items.grammar: "Erst am 1. Juli 1890 kam sie … zu Deutschland": erst + time expression means "not until / only then", stressing that something happened later than one might expect – unlike nur, which limits quantity. 【erst 表示“直到……才”】
questions: Welches Interesse hatte Bismarck daran, den Vertrag schlechtzumachen?
